On neuromorphic chips, spiking neural networks (SNNs)
consume far less energy than artificial neural networks
(ANNs), but the limited memory of these chips requires
low-bit synaptic weights and membrane potentials. Exist-
ing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods provide them
without retraining and, like those for ANNs, minimize nu-
merical errors such as the mean squared error (MSE). In
an SNN, however, a quantization error reaches later layers
only through the spikes it flips. We find that errors of equal
MSE can cause very different accuracy losses, whereas er-
rors that flip the same fraction of spikes cause the same loss.

simulating the downstream neurons and minimizing their

low-bit synaptic weights and membrane potentials. Exist-
ing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods provide them

an SNN, however, a quantization error reaches later layers
only through the spikes it flips. We find that errors of equal
MSE can cause very different accuracy losses, whereas er-
rors that flip the same fraction of spikes cause the same loss.
We therefore proposeSpikeQ, a spike-guided PTQ frame-
work. For weights, we select the level of each weight by
simulating the downstream neurons and minimizing their

evidence.excerpt:
reset, whereas neuromorphic
chips compare the threshold with the membrane potential
stored at a fixed bit width. We target this pre-fire quanti-
zation and build a reset-aware grid that places the thresh-
old on a rounding boundary, so rounding never flips the
spike at the current time step. We evaluate SpikeQ on seven
benchmarks of image classification, semantic segmentation,
and object detection. With 2-bit pre-fire membrane poten-
tials, every existing grid collapses, whereas SpikeQ retains
most of the full-precision accuracy. With both at 4 bits, the
models stay within 2.59 points of full precision, shrink their
memory footprint 7.8–7.9×, and use 6.4–6.9×less energy.

Quantizing the weights changes the input current, the mem-
brane potential, and the spikes of the downstream neuron
(Fig. 2(a)). Existing methods select the weight levels that
minimize the error of the input current or the membrane
potential, yet the resulting spikes can still differ from the
full-precision ones (Fig. 3). SpikeQ instead takes the spikes
as the optimization target and selects the weight levels that
minimize the spike error.

evidence.excerpt:
Models and calibration.All experiments run on
NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80 GB of memory. The CIFAR
models and both SDT models use LIF neurons, and
SEW-ResNet-18 uses IF neurons. Weight calibration uses
a single seed, and on CIFAR-10 at W2, SpikeQ averages
90.52±0.19over three calibration seeds. All COCO
results, including full precision, are evaluated in FP32 with
TF32 disabled.
Weight quantization.Weights are quantized per output
channel. GPTQ and SBC use their default min-max grids,
and GPTAQ usesα= 0.25, the default of its official im-
plementation. BRECQ, PTQ4SNN, and SpikeQ share the
same clipping search for the weight grid, which minimizes
theL 2.4 weight error, so they differ only in the selected lev-
els. BRECQ and PTQ4SNN use 20k reconstruction itera-
tions (5k on COCO). On COCO, all methods keep the first
layer and the detection head at 8 bits with round-to-nearest.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Final results are reported as top-1 accuracy, mIoU, and AP/AP50 on held-out benchmark evaluation sets, which do not use the spike-matching calibration objectives.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Standard ground-truth task metrics (top-1 accuracy, mIoU, AP/AP50) on benchmark validation/test sets.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: The spike-count, margin, and population losses computed against full-precision and local spike references during calibration.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Claims that spike preservation drives downstream task fidelity and that threshold anchoring prevents low-bit pre-fire collapse are directly corroborated by empirical results (e.g., maintaining competitive mIoU and accuracy at 2-bit where conventional methods collapse).
primary.evaluation_assessment: The evaluation is rigorous and extensive, benchmarking pre-fire and post-reset quantization across seven distinct vision datasets and tasks (classification, segmentation, detection) and multiple SNN architectures, complete with ablations on each loss/grid component, energy modeling, and comparison against seven PTQ baselines.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Final model evaluation relies on standard ground-truth benchmark metrics across ImageNet, CIFAR, VOC 2012, ADE20K, and COCO validation sets, entirely separate from the local spike-matching calibration objective.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Standard ground-truth task metrics (top-1 classification accuracy, mIoU, AP/AP50) evaluated on full held-out test/validation datasets.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Spike-count loss, margin loss, and population loss computed on a small unlabeled calibration set (1,024 images for weights, 256 for membrane grids).

primary.limitations: The authors observe performance degradation when jointly compressing to 2-bit on complex tasks due to accumulating flipped spikes, and note that pre-fire quantization under soft reset requires a wider grid spanning above the threshold.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly detailed, specifying a discrete coordinate-search optimization for weights with spike count, margin, and population terms alongside a mathematically proven threshold-anchoring grid design that ensures pre-fire rounding avoids flipping spikes and aligns post-reset states to exact grid levels.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript presents sound theoretical and empirical justifications for departing from standard MSE-based PTQ objectives in spiking networks, executes a comprehensive set of controlled experiments, and clearly details all implementation aspects.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces SpikeQ, a spike-guided post-training quantization framework for spiking neural networks that quantizes weights by minimizing downstream spike errors and quantizes pre-fire membrane potentials using threshold-anchored, reset-aware grids.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The manuscript presents sound theoretical and empirical justifications for departing from standard MSE-based PTQ objectives in spiking networks, executes a comprehensive set of controlled experiments, and clearly details all implementation aspects.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors observe performance degradation when jointly compressing to 2-bit on complex tasks due to accumulating flipped spikes, and note that pre-fire quantization under soft reset requires a wider grid spanning above the threshold.
